title: IP Bans Explained: What Discord, Roblox, TikTok, Reddit and Twitter Actually Block
author: IP Ready
excerpt: An IP ban blocks the network, not the account. How each major platform uses them, why a VPN often makes things worse, and the order of fixes that actually works.
body:
'You're banned' and 'your IP is banned' are different sentences. An account ban travels with your credentials — an IP ban travels with your network, catching everyone and everything behind that address. Knowing which one hit you determines everything about the fix, so this guide maps out how the major platforms really use IP bans and what to do when one lands on you, fairly or not.

What an IP Ban Is (and Isn't)

When a platform bans your IP, its servers stop trusting requests from that address — or every address in its range. The effect ranges from a permanent loop of verification challenges to a flat 'you cannot view this page'.

Two consequences surprise people:

  • Shared addresses make bans contagious. On carrier-grade NAT (most mobile connections), dorm networks, and offices, thousands of users share one public IP. One person's spam can network-ban a whole building.
  • An IP ban rarely works alone. Platforms layer it with device fingerprints, cookies, and behavioral history. That is why simply changing address sometimes 'doesn't work' — the ban was never only about the address.

What Each Platform Actually Does

PlatformTypical IP ban behaviorWhat usually triggers it
DiscordMostly server-level bans covering account and IP; platform-wide bans for raids and ToS violationsSpam, raid tools, ban evasion with alts
RobloxIP and device signals combined, aimed at stopping alt accountsEvasion after a warning, exploitation, trade scams
TikTokRarely announced outright; appears as shadow restrictions and failed loginsMultiple accounts per address, engagement automation
RedditSubreddit bans extend to IPs; site-wide bans target evasion networksVote manipulation, ban evasion, spam rings
Twitter / XLogin challenges and account locks tied to suspicious addressesAggressive automation, login from flagged exits

The pattern behind the table: platforms IP-ban when they believe the network is the source of the problem — bulk abuse, evasion attempts, or addresses with a bad reputation.

Does a VPN Bypass an IP Ban?

Sometimes it restores reachability — and just as often it makes things worse. Here is the honest mechanics:

  • Datacenter VPN exits are themselves heavily flagged. Millions of people rotate through the same addresses. Moving from your banned home IP to a busy VPN exit trades one bad reputation for another, and many platforms show extra challenges specifically on known VPN ranges.
  • Evasion can escalate the ban. Most platforms treat creating a new account to bypass a ban as a separate violation, and they link the new account back through device and behavioral fingerprints even when the IP changes.
  • Appeals are the sanctioned route. If the ban was a mistake — and shared-IP collateral damage is common — the platform's appeal process is the fix that does not come back to bite you.

Where a clean IP genuinely helps is the legitimate case: your household, dorm, or office was range-banned because of someone else's behavior. Getting your own clean exit (a fresh lease from your ISP, or a static residential line) plus an appeal that says 'I share a network with the offender' resolves most of these.

The Fix Order That Works

1. Identify the ban type. Test from a different network (phone on mobile data). If you are fine there, the ban is on your IP — not your account. That distinction is exactly what the appeal needs to say.

2. Look at your own address before you claim innocence. Run a scan. If the report shows blacklist hits or abuse history on your exit, the platform acted on evidence, and your appeal should acknowledge and fix the cause rather than dispute the ban.

3. Appeal with the right facts. 'Banned by mistake — here is the shared-network situation, and here is a fresh risk report of my connection' is a solvable ticket. 'Unban me' is not.

4. If you need a new exit, change one thing at a time. A clean static residential IP, the same device, the same browser — one variable changed, then observe. Changing address, device, and account simultaneously is precisely the pattern evasion detection looks for.

Avoiding the Next False Ban

  • Scan your IP before high-stakes sessions, not after something breaks.
  • Keep one account per network where the platform is strict — account-per-IP is the pattern bulk abuse creates.
  • Avoid free VPN exits for account work; their reputation is already spent.
  • If you share a network, assume you share its reputation too.

Start with a scan — it takes the guesswork out of step 2. For the platform people hit most, see the Discord-specific guide at how Discord IP bans work and how to fix them, and if your address shows blacklist history, read how to check and remove a blacklisted IP.
